title: Why NOT solve the dual-write problem with a distributed/global transaction across PostgreSQL and Kafka, and what is the key distinction between atomicity (all commit together) and recoverability (durable local transactions + explicit eventual consistency + safe retries + reconciliation) — i.e. which invariants truly need synchronous atomicity?
shortTitle: Why NOT solve the dual-write problem with a distributed transaction across PostgreSQL and Kafka, and what is the difference between atomicity and recoverability?

s1_definition.profdef: The dual-write problem — writing to a database and publishing to Kafka in one operation — tempts engineers to reach for a distributed transaction such as two-phase commit (2PC) that spans both systems. This is a poor solution because Kafka does not participate well in XA transactions, 2PC is slow and holds locks across a network round trip, the transaction coordinator becomes a single point of failure, and the whole thing blocks when any participant is slow or down. The better model distinguishes atomicity (all participants commit together, synchronously) from recoverability (each system commits its own durable local transaction, and consistency is reached afterward through eventual consistency, safe idempotent retries, and reconciliation). Most invariants in a distributed system need only recoverability; true synchronous atomicity is needed only for a narrow set of invariants that must hold at a single instant within one data store.
s1_definition.analogy: Rajesh's transfer at National Bank of India must update the ledger and send an event. One idea is to make the ledger clerk and the Kafka courier shake hands and promise "we both finish together or both cancel" — a distributed transaction. But this means the clerk cannot close his ledger until the courier confirms, and if the courier is stuck in traffic the clerk is frozen mid-transaction, holding the whole counter hostage. The smarter bank way is: the clerk finishes his own ledger entry durably and immediately (a local transaction), and a separate reliable process makes sure the event eventually goes out, with retries, and a nightly reconciliation that cross-checks the ledger against the events to catch any mismatch. The money moving between two accounts inside the same ledger genuinely must be atomic; the ledger-plus-event does not — it only needs to become consistent eventually and be reconcilable.
s1_definition.oneliner: Do not span two systems with a distributed transaction for the dual write — commit each system's own local transaction and reach consistency through eventual consistency, idempotent retries, and reconciliation, reserving true atomicity for invariants inside a single store.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The dual-write problem — writing to a database and publishing to Kafka in one operation — tempts engineers to reach for a distributed transaction such as two-phase commit (2PC) that spans both systems. This is a poor solution because Kafka does not participate well in XA transactions, 2PC is slow and holds locks across a network round trip, the transaction coordinator becomes a single point of failure, and the whole thing blocks when any participant is slow or down. The better model distinguishes atomicity (all participants commit together, synchronously) from recoverability (each system commits its own durable local transaction, and consistency is reached afterward through eventual consistency, safe idempotent retries, and reconciliation). Most invariants in a distributed system need only recoverability; true synchronous atomicity is needed only for a narrow set of invariants that must hold at a single instant within one data store.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Rajesh's transfer at National Bank of India must update the ledger and send an event. One idea is to make the ledger clerk and the Kafka courier shake hands and promise "we both finish together or both cancel" — a distributed transaction. But this means the clerk cannot close his ledger until the courier confirms, and if the courier is stuck in traffic the clerk is frozen mid-transaction, holding the whole counter hostage. The smarter bank way is: the clerk finishes his own ledger entry durably and immediately (a local transaction), and a separate reliable process makes sure the event eventually goes out, with retries, and a nightly reconciliation that cross-checks the ledger against the events to catch any mismatch. The money moving between two accounts inside the same ledger genuinely must be atomic; the ledger-plus-event does not — it only needs to become consistent eventually and be reconcilable.

**One line to remember:** Do not span two systems with a distributed transaction for the dual write — commit each system's own local transaction and reach consistency through eventual consistency, idempotent retries, and reconciliation, reserving true atomicity for invariants inside a single store.

sections.s2_technical:
Atomicity in the ACID sense means a set of operations either all commit or all roll back, with no partial state ever visible. A distributed transaction tries to extend this across multiple systems using a protocol like two-phase commit. In 2PC a coordinator asks every participant "can you commit?" (the prepare phase), and if all say yes it tells them all "commit" (the commit phase). This sounds clean but has severe problems in practice.

First, Kafka is not designed as an XA resource manager; forcing it into a global transaction is awkward and not how it is meant to be used. Second, 2PC is slow because it requires multiple network round trips and every participant must hold its locks from prepare until commit, which across a network can be a long time, killing throughput. Third, the coordinator is a single point of failure: if it crashes after participants have prepared but before it sends commit, participants are stuck in an in-doubt state holding locks, blocked, until the coordinator recovers. Fourth, availability suffers — if any one participant is down, the whole transaction cannot complete, so you have coupled the availability of your database and your broker, making the combined system less available than either alone. For a high-throughput banking system these costs are unacceptable.

The key conceptual shift is from atomicity to recoverability. Recoverability means each system performs a durable local transaction that it can commit independently and quickly, and the overall consistency between systems is achieved after the fact rather than at a single instant. The ingredients are: durable local transactions (the database commit and, separately, the event record are each individually durable, as in the outbox pattern), explicit eventual consistency (the system acknowledges that for a brief window the two systems may differ, and that is acceptable), safe retries (operations are idempotent so re-running them after a failure is harmless), and reconciliation (a periodic process compares the two systems and fixes or alerts on drift).

A small code example of a safe retry is an idempotent apply keyed by a business id: `if (ledger.alreadyApplied(txnId)) return; ledger.apply(txnId, amount);` so retrying the same transfer id does nothing the second time. A small example of reconciliation is a nightly job that does `for each committed transfer, assert an event exists; else re-publish` and `for each event, assert a committed transfer exists; else alert`.

The senior insight is deciding which invariants truly need synchronous atomicity. The invariant "debit and credit of a single transfer must both happen or neither" absolutely needs atomicity, but it lives entirely inside one database, so a single local transaction gives it for free — no distributed transaction needed. The invariant "a transfer and its published event must both exist" does not need to hold at a single instant; it only needs to hold eventually, so recoverability via outbox plus retries plus reconciliation is the right tool. The mistake juniors make is treating every cross-system relationship as if it needs instantaneous atomicity, which forces them toward distributed transactions and all their pathologies. The discipline is to keep atomic invariants inside a single store and make everything crossing a system boundary eventually consistent and reconcilable.
sections.s3_banking:
At National Bank of India, a transfer debits Rajesh, credits Priya, and must emit a TransferCompleted event for downstream services.

Problem 1 — The frozen counter. An architect proposed wrapping the database write and the Kafka publish in a two-phase commit. During a Kafka broker slowdown, every transfer began hanging: the database held locks waiting for Kafka to confirm the prepare phase, connection pools exhausted, and the entire transfer counter froze even though the database itself was perfectly healthy. This is exactly why distributed transactions across heterogeneous systems are dangerous — they couple availability and hold locks across the network.

Problem 2 — The invariant confusion. The team realized they had conflated two different invariants. The debit-equals-credit invariant must be atomic, but it lives inside one database, so one local transaction handles it. The transfer-has-an-event invariant was being forced into the same synchronous atomic boundary even though it only needs to be true eventually.

The fix: commit the debit and credit in one local database transaction (true atomicity, single store). Record the event durably too (outbox) and let it flow with safe retries. Run a reconciliation job that checks every committed transfer has an event and re-publishes any gaps.

The code will have a `Ledger` that applies a transfer atomically and idempotently by transfer id, an `EventStore` that durably records events, a `Reconciler` that compares ledger and events and repairs gaps, and a demo that applies a transfer, simulates a missing event, and shows reconciliation repairing it without any distributed transaction.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: TXN-1 transfers 50,000 from Rajesh to Priya; TXN-2 transfers 10,000 but its event is lost.

Step 1 — TXN-1 enters the ledger. Debit and credit and the transfer record all commit in one local transaction — true atomicity inside a single store, no distributed transaction. Rajesh drops to 950,000, Priya rises to 300,000.

Step 2 — The event for TXN-1 is recorded durably in a separate write. The two systems now agree.

Step 3 — TXN-1 is retried with the same id. The ledger sees the id already applied and does nothing — a safe idempotent retry, so no double debit.

Step 4 — TXN-2 commits in the ledger, but the process dies before recording its event. Now the ledger and the event store disagree: the transfer happened but no event exists. This is the temporary inconsistency that eventual consistency tolerates.

Step 5 — The nightly reconciler runs. It walks every committed transfer and checks for a matching event. It finds TXN-2 has none, re-records the event, and logs the repair. The two systems are consistent again — recoverability, not atomicity, fixed the gap.

```
2026-10-24 16:41:30 [INFO] Ledger committed TXN-1 amount 50000 (atomic single-store debit+credit)
2026-10-24 16:41:30 [INFO] Event recorded for TXN-1
2026-10-24 16:41:30 [INFO] --- retry same TXN-1 (should be a no-op) ---
2026-10-24 16:41:30 [WARNING] TXN TXN-1 already applied — no-op (idempotent)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The dual-write problem tempts people to wrap the database write and the Kafka publish in a distributed transaction such as two-phase commit, but I avoid that deliberately. Kafka is not meant to be an XA resource, two-phase commit is slow because it holds locks across network round trips, the transaction coordinator is a single point of failure that can leave participants stuck in-doubt holding locks, and most importantly it couples the availability of my database and my broker, so if Kafka is slow my database transactions freeze even though the database is perfectly healthy. In a banking system that trade is unacceptable.

The conceptual key is distinguishing atomicity from recoverability. Atomicity means all participants commit together at a single instant, with no partial state ever visible. Recoverability means each system commits its own durable local transaction quickly and independently, and overall consistency is reached afterward through explicit eventual consistency, idempotent retries that are safe to repeat, and a reconciliation process that compares the systems and repairs any drift. The insight is that most cross-system relationships only need recoverability, not instantaneous atomicity.

The question I always ask is which invariant truly needs synchronous atomicity. In my transfer service the invariant that the debit and the credit must both happen or neither absolutely needs atomicity, but it lives entirely inside one database, so a single local transaction gives it for free with no distributed transaction at all. The invariant that a transfer and its published event must both exist does not need to hold at a single instant; it only needs to hold eventually, so I use the outbox pattern for durable events, idempotent keys so retries are safe, and a nightly reconciler that finds any committed transfer missing an event and re-publishes it.

The mistake I have seen juniors make is treating every cross-system relationship as if it needs instantaneous atomicity, which pushes them toward distributed transactions and all their pathologies. The discipline is to keep atomic invariants inside a single store and make everything that crosses a system boundary eventually consistent and reconcilable.

The one-line summary I give is: never span two systems with a distributed transaction for the dual write; commit each system's own local transaction and reach consistency through eventual consistency, idempotent retries, and reconciliation, reserving true synchronous atomicity for invariants that live inside one data store.
